########## AGENTS.md
# AGENTS.md

Structure and conventions for anyone, human or agent, working in this repository.

## Phases

Work is organised into phases. Each phase maps to one milestone (`vX.Y.Z`) and one `phase-N` label. A phase ends when its milestone closes.

## Tracks

If the project splits into more than one workstream running in parallel, each gets a `track-*` label (for example `track-a`, `track-b`). Not in use until that happens.

## The wayfinder protocol

Each phase opens with one `wayfinder:map` issue: the phase's single source of truth for what's known, decided, and next.

A map issue body has three sections, kept up to date as children close:

- **Fog** — open unknowns.
- **Decisions so far** — what's been settled, and why.
- **Frontier** — the next unblocked tickets.

Child tickets hang off the map issue with a `Part of: #n` line, and carry one of:

- `wayfinder:research` — investigate and report back, no implementation.
- `wayfinder:grilling` — stress-test a plan or decision before committing to it.
- `wayfinder:prototype` — throwaway build to answer a design question.
- `wayfinder:task` — a concrete, scoped piece of work.

## Labels

- Phase: `phase-0`, `phase-1`, and so on.
- Track: `track-a`, `track-b`, added once more than one workstream exists.
- Wayfinder: `wayfinder:map`, `wayfinder:research`, `wayfinder:grilling`, `wayfinder:prototype`, `wayfinder:task`.
- Severity: `p1`, `p2`, `p3`.
- Workflow: `needs-decision`, `needs-repro`, `needs-research`, `ready-for-agent`, `pending-release`.
- Defaults: `bug`, `documentation`, `enhancement`.

## Research tracks

Output of a `wayfinder:research` ticket lands in `docs/research/issue-<n>-<slug>.md`. Every file ends with a recommendation. A recommendation that's adopted gets promoted to a numbered ADR in `docs/adr/`.

## Architecture decisions

`docs/adr/` holds numbered ADRs, one decision per file, starting from `docs/adr/0000-template.md`. The index lives in `docs/adr/README.md` and must stay in sync with the files present.

## Issues

- Use the templates in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`. Blank issues are disabled, feature ideas and questions go to Discussions instead.
- Keep bug reports short: steps to reproduce, expected versus actual behaviour, environment. No root-cause guesses or patches in the report itself.

## Pull requests

- Title: Conventional Commits, with scope where it helps, for example `feat(cli): add status command (#12)`.
- Body: *What this does*, *Why*, and a checklist (tests pass, docs updated if behaviour changed, ADR added if touching architecture).
- Reference the issue with `refs #n`, not `closes #n`. The maintainer closes issues on merge.
- Small commits, Conventional Commits, no co-author trailers.

## House style

- British English throughout.
- No em dashes.
- Short and direct. No filler, no hedging.

## Documents

Reference materials go in `/materials/`, which is gitignored and never committed.

########## AGENTS.md
# Agent guide

How an engineering agent should work in this repo.

## Skills

### Issue tracker

Issues and specs live in this repo's GitHub Issues. See
[`docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`](docs/agents/issue-tracker.md).

### Domain docs

Single-context layout: [`CONTEXT.md`](CONTEXT.md) and [`docs/adr/`](docs/adr) at
the repo root. See [`docs/agents/domain.md`](docs/agents/domain.md).

### Wayfinder

Each phase opens with a `wayfinder:map` issue. Research and grilling tickets
hang off it and resolve into ADRs before build tickets start. The frontier is
the set of open child tickets with no open blocker.

## Invariants

These do not change without an ADR that supersedes this list.

### One maintainer

Mnemosyne has a single maintainer, Nabil Shah. Every commit, issue, and pull
request is authored by him. External pull requests are not merged; they are
declined politely and closed. No commit carries a co-author trailer.

### `mnem-store` is offline and model-free

Nothing in `mnem-store` opens a network connection or calls a model. The
substrate is deterministic. `deny.toml` bans every network, TLS and
async-runtime crate from the workspace tree, and the `deny` CI job enforces it;
this is the check ADR-0004 promised. The semantic layer (Era 2) lives behind a
trait, in a separate crate, and its default implementation is a local model.

### The on-disk format changes only by the rules in ADR-0007

`config` carries a `format_version` integer, on its own track from the software
SemVer. An additive format change (a new object kind, a new optional field)
bumps `format_version`. A change that would make an older reader misread an
existing object bumps `format_version` and ships `mnem migrate`. A newer release
opens any older store it declares support for; an older release refuses a newer
store with a clear message. The software bump that carries a `format_version`
change is a MINOR from `0.1.0` on, and a `0.0.x` bump while the roadmap is still
in `0.0.x` (ADR-0010).

### A commit's id does not include its signature

An object's id is the BLAKE3 hash of its canonical bytes (ADR-0005). A commit's
hashed bytes are `{kind, parents, state, message, author, time}`. Signatures live
in a side table. Signing, re-signing, or adding a signature never changes any
id, and signing is never required by any operation.

### The human is always the gate in Era 2

When the review model lands, an approval is only ever given by a person or an
explicit policy they configured. A critic agent advises; it never approves or
vetoes on its own.

## House style

British English. Plain, short sentences. No marketing tone in commits, issues,
or ADRs. No em dashes.

Commit messages and pull request titles follow Conventional Commits (ADR-0011):
`<type>(<scope>): <description>`, lowercase, imperative, concise, for example
`feat(core): add the commit object and its content hash`. The body, when
present, stays plain and explains why. Reference an issue with `refs #<n>` in

The search points to **τ-Voice**, the full-duplex voice extension of τ²-bench, which is the benchmark you're looking for.

- **Paper:** τ-Voice is on arXiv as 2603.13686 (cs.SD), by Soham Ray, Keshav Dhandhania, Victor Barres, and Karthik Narasimhan. It was also accepted as an ICML 2026 poster. Code is available at https://github.com/sierra-research/tau2-bench.
- **What it measures:** The benchmark pairs verifiable task completion with full-duplex interaction and realistic audio. Its authors note that earlier work tested tool use only in text, and that full-duplex benchmarks used synthetic tasks without real tool calls. It is the first to combine all three and enables direct comparison between voice and text agent performance on grounded tasks.
- **Voice simulator:** The paper introduces a voice user simulator with varied accents, audio environments, and turn-taking dynamics. It separates simulation time from wall-clock time, which lets it use a stronger LLM for the user side.
- **Lineage:** The core τ²-bench paper is arXiv 2506.07982, per a third-party summary site, and it added a telecom dual-control domain. The τ³-bench release in the same repo adds voice full-duplex evaluation and a banking knowledge domain. The repo's citation block lists τ-Knowledge (arXiv 2603.04370) for the knowledge domain.
- **Related work:** Full-Duplex-Bench-v3 (arXiv 2604.04847, NVIDIA and National Taiwan University) is a separate benchmark for tool use by full-duplex voice agents. It uses real human audio with disfluencies and chained API calls.

The search turned up a paper introducing EVA-Bench, a ServiceNow framework for evaluating voice agents, plus a secondary summary.

- **Method:** The framework runs automated, multi-turn bot-to-bot audio conversations and includes a validation step that catches user-simulator errors and regenerates those conversations. About 12 % of trials required reruns, almost entirely due to user behavioral drift.
- **Cascade vs. speech-to-speech:** Its main purpose is comparing the two architectures under the same conditions. It orchestrates parallel audio sessions over a live WebSocket, enabling the evaluation of both cascade and audio-native architectures under identical conditions.
- **Metrics:** It defines an accuracy score (EVA-A) and an experience score (EVA-X). The accuracy score covers task completion and faithfulness, and the experience score covers conciseness, turn-taking, and naturalness. One secondary summary says bots which are great at following rules often struggle to sound human, and vice versa.
- **Results:** One summary reports that across 213 enterprise scenarios and 12 systems, no system exceeds 0.5 on both the accuracy and experience scores, and that it reveals robustness gaps under accent/noise perturbations. The framework is open-source.
- **Discrepancy:** The secondary summary (voiceaispace) describes an earlier or different version: 50 validated airline scenarios, and it names Gemini 1.5 and Claude 3 as judges. The hyper.ai summary describes the broader 213-scenario version. I did not check the arXiv paper directly, so the arXiv listing is the authoritative source for the final numbers.

EnterpriseOps-Gym is a ServiceNow benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on multi-step enterprise work. The paper is arXiv 2603.13594, dated March 13, 2026.

- **Setup:** The benchmark uses a containerized sandbox with 164 database tables and 512 functional tools. It spans eight interconnected ecosystems, from productivity tools like email, calendar, Teams, and Drive to HR, IT service management, and customer service management, plus a hybrid category for cross-domain tasks.
- **Tasks:** The benchmark has 1,150 expert-authored tasks, including 30 infeasible scenarios that check whether agents refuse unsatisfiable requests without side effects.
- **Grading:** Agents are scored on final environment state using SQL verifiers, not on the transcript. A task counts as a success only when every verifier over the resulting state passes.
- **Results:** The Hugging Face dataset card reports a best model performance: 34.1% success rate. I did not confirm whether this figure is current.
- **ServiceNow's framing:** ServiceNow describes it as the first component of NOWAI-Bench. Its blog says the models were tested without any platform support, so the results measure raw model capability. The company also calls it the most comprehensive benchmark to date, which is a vendor claim.
- **Independent leaderboard:** Artificial Analysis runs its own version, EnterpriseOps-Gym-AA, which it announced on July 8, 2026. Its headline metric is the strict task success rate.

Links: paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.13594), project site (https://enterpriseops-gym.github.io/), dataset (https://huggingface.co/datasets/ServiceNow-AI/EnterpriseOps-Gym).

Smart Turn is Pipecat's open-source turn-detection model, and v3 is the version Pipecat's docs recommend. The search results don't show anything dated 2026 specifically, so I can't confirm the latest release status.

- **Purpose and approach:** The model decides when a speaker has finished and the agent should reply, using acoustic and linguistic cues rather than only speech/non-speech detection. Most voice agents today use voice activity detection (VAD) as the basis for turn detection. VAD segments audio into "speech" and "non-speech" segments.
- **Licensing:** The GitHub repo describes a truly open model (BSD 2-clause license).
- **Performance and footprint:** The repo says it runs in as little as 10ms on some CPUs, and under 100ms on most cloud instances and comes in CPU (8MB quantized) and GPU (32MB unquantized) versions. It is meant to pair with Silero VAD, so it only runs during silences.
- **Languages:** The repo lists support for 23 languages.
- **Architecture:** The Hugging Face card for v3.x describes a Whisper Tiny encoder backbone with a shallow linear classifier head and about 8M parameters. A separate third-party listing describes a Wav2Vec2-BERT backbone, which appears to be an older version, so the sources conflict on architecture.
- **Pipecat integration:** Pipecat's docs say as of v0.0.102, TurnAnalyzerUserTurnStopStrategy with LocalSmartTurnAnalyzerV3 is the default user turn stop strategy in Pipecat. The weights ship with the package, so no separate download is needed.
- **Version note:** The GitHub README is titled Smart Turn v3.2, so v3 has had point releases since the docs were written.

# MASA-Safe-RL

![MASA-Safe-RL](images/logo_large.png)

[View Documentation](https://sacktock.github.io/MASA-Safe-RL)

______________________________________________________________________

Welcome to MASA-Safe-RL, the Multi and Single Agent (MASA) Safe Reinforcement Learning library. The primary goal of this library is to develop a set of common constraints and environments for safe reinforcement learning research, built on top of the popular [gymnasium](https://gymnasium.farama.org/) interface. We span, CMPDs, probabilistic constraints, Reach-Avoid and LTL-Safety (DFA) properties.

The library is in very early stage development and we greatly appreciate and encourage feedback from the community about what they would like to see implemented. Currently we provide a set of basic tabular algroithms for safe RL, but we provide a modular and resuable framework for developing more complex algorithms and constraints.

If you use MASA-Safe-RL in your research please cite it in your publications.

```bibtex
@misc{Goodall2025MASASafeRL,

}

## Quick Start

### Installation

#### Prequisites

Python 3.13+ is required (3.13 recommended).

#### Installation with conda

- Install conda, e.g., via [anaconda](https://anaconda.org/channels/anaconda/packages/conda/overview).
- Clone the repo:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/sacktock/MASA-Safe-RL.git
cd MASA-Safe-RL
```

- Create a conda virtual environment:

```bash
conda env create --name masa --file conda-environment.yaml
conda activate masa
```

- Install dependencies:

```bash
pip install -e .
```

#### Installation with uv

`uv sync` installs only base dependency package from the repository root.

**Easiest way to install all dependencies:** All dependency groups (docs and GPU support for CUDA13): `uv sync --all-groups --no-group cuda12`.

Alternatively, `uv sync --all-groups --no-group cuda13` if your system only supports CUDA 12.

More minimal ways of installing dependency groups:

- For building docs, use `uv sync --group docs` from the repository root.
- Adding GPU support for Jax: `uv sync --group cuda13` (or `cuda12` if CUDA 13 is not supported by your device)

#### Installation with PyPI

MASA-Safe-RL is now available on PyPI: [MASA-Safe-RL](https://pypi.org/project/MASA-Safe-RL/).

```bash
pip install -U MASA-Safe-RL
```

The search returned ten copies of the same Hugging Face model card, all titled "Kronos: A Foundation Model for the Language of Financial Markets." None of them is an arXiv page, and none is clearly the official upstream repo, so I can't confirm the arXiv or GitHub links from these results.

The model card describes Kronos as a family of decoder-only models pre-trained on K-line sequences, which are candlestick data. It uses a tokenizer that converts OHLCV data into discrete tokens, followed by an autoregressive Transformer. The pre-training corpus covers over 12 billion K-line records from 45 global exchanges. The stated zero-shot tasks are price series forecasting, volatility forecasting, and synthetic data generation. The card also says all models are readily accessible from the Hugging Face Hub.

Because the copies are identical and some come from personal accounts (for example, usernames like "fdfsdfdsf" and "PeachyVibes"), treat them as mirrors rather than authoritative sources. To verify the model and find the paper, check the official GitHub and arXiv listings directly.

The search turned up the core papers but nothing from 2026, and little from 2025 beyond one LOBFrame paper.

- **DeepLOB (2018/2019):** Zhang, Zohren and Roberts built a CNN-plus-LSTM model for LOB mid-price moves. It reported F1 scores of 77.66% at k=10 on the FI-2010 benchmark, and it was tested on one year market quotes from the London Stock Exchange.
- **FI-2010 benchmark (2017):** The dataset paper by Ntakaris et al. describes a mid-price forecasting protocol built on NASDAQ OMX Nordic ITCH data, covering ten trading days for five stocks.
- **LOBCAST (2023 preprint):** Prata et al. examine the robustness and generalizability of fifteen state-of-the-art DL models with an open-source framework that incorporates data preprocessing, DL model training, evaluation and profit analysis. Their main finding is that all models exhibit a significant performance drop when exposed to new data.
- **LOBFrame (Quantitative Finance, 2025):** Briola, Bartolucci and Aste published a peer-reviewed version in 2025 that releases 'LOBFrame', an open-source code base to efficiently process large-scale Limit Order Book data. They also report that the stocks' microstructural characteristics influence the efficacy of deep learning methods, which bears on cross-stock generalization.

The paper is "Hyperparameters in Reinforcement Learning and How To Tune Them" by Theresa Eimer, Marius Lindauer, and Roberta Raileanu, published at ICML 2023 (PMLR vol. 202, pp. 9104–9149). The authors show that RL hyperparameter choices can substantially affect final performance and sample efficiency, and that the hyperparameter landscape can depend heavily on the tuning seed, which may lead to overfitting. To address this, they recommend borrowing AutoML practices, including keeping tuning seeds separate from testing seeds, and running principled hyperparameter optimization over a broad search space (as well as principled hyperparameter optimization (HPO) across a broad search space.).

The paper is also on arXiv (2306.01324), and a talk on it was given at ICML in July 2023. The search results did not include the paper's full body text, so details of the specific experiments and tuning recommendations beyond the abstract would need to be checked in the PDF.

The paper you're likely thinking of is **"Probabilistic Shielding for Safe Reinforcement Learning"** by Edwin Hamel-De le Court, Francesco Belardinelli, and Alexander W. Goodall. It's on arXiv as 2503.07671 (March 2025) and was published at AAAI 2025. Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 39(15), 16091-16099.

The paper targets settings where the safety dynamics of an MDP are known and safety is an undiscounted probabilistic avoidance property. Its method offers strict formal guarantees and scales better than linear-programming approaches, which the authors say have limited scaling. The approach uses state augmentation plus a shield that limits which actions the agent can take. The authors state that this provides a strict formal safety guarantee that the agent stays safe at training and test time.

Two related works by the same group:
- **Goodall & Belardinelli (arXiv 2402.00816, Feb 2024):** "Leveraging Approximate Model-based Shielding for Probabilistic Safety Guarantees in Continuous Environments." It covers settings where the safety-relevant dynamics aren't known in advance. Approximate Model-based Shielding (AMBS) is the framework it uses.
- **ProSh (arXiv 2510.15720):** by Hamel-De le Court, Ohlmann, and Belardinelli, not Goodall. It proposes Probabilistic Shielding via Risk Augmentation (ProSh), a model-free algorithm for safe reinforcement learning under cost constraints.

I only ran one search, so I didn't verify the full text of each paper.

The search turned up the NeurIPS 2021 paper "Deep RL at the Edge of the Statistical Precipice" and its open-source library, rliable.

- **Core argument:** The authors argue that point estimates ignore sampling uncertainty when only a few runs are available. They say statistical uncertainty needs to be considered, especially with only a few training runs, for deep RL evaluation to be reliable.
- **Stratified bootstrap CIs:** The method treats any aggregate metric from finite runs as a random variable and estimates its spread. Bootstrap samples are built by drawing scores with replacement, proportionately from each task. The CIs draw on the scores on combined runs across tasks. One example: three runs each on Atari 100k, which contains 26 tasks, yields 78 sample scores for uncertainty estimation.
- **Better aggregate metrics:** The paper proposes the interquartile mean (IQM) and probability of improvement. The IQM is robust to outlier scores but more statistically efficient than median, computed over the middle 50% of combined runs. The mean, by contrast, can be dominated by a few outlier tasks.
- **Performance profiles:** These plot the score distribution across all runs and tasks with uncertainty estimates using stratified bootstrap confidence bands.
- **Library:** rliable supports stratified bootstrap CIs, performance profiles, IQM, optimality gap, and probability of improvement. The package is installable via pip install -U rliable, and a colab notebook demonstrates use on Atari 100k, ALE, DM Control and Procgen.

The search didn't turn up anything specific to reinforcement learning or CPU-only RL performance, so the findings below cover JAX on Apple Silicon generally.

- **Official jax-metal looks stale.** An Apple Developer Forums post says in DEC 2025 the Jax maintainers have closed all issues citing No active development on Jax-metal. That's the poster's account, not an official statement. The PyPI page's version table tops out at 0.1.1, which targets jaxlib 0.4.34, and it describes the plugin as experimental and not all JAX functionality may be supported.
- **Third-party alternatives are active.** metaljax is a Metal backend in beta, and its author says transformer training steps run within a few percent of PyTorch's MPS backend. It also notes coverage gaps remain. jax-mps uses MLX and the last push was on Apr 22, 2026. Its own benchmark reports a ~3.7x speed-up over the CPU backend when training a simple ResNet18 model on CIFAR-10 using an M4 MacBook Air. That's a vendor-reported result for a supervised CNN, not RL.
- **CPU-vs-GPU data is limited.** One Japanese blog post on an M2 found the Metal plugin usable, but its timing example was a 1000×1000 matrix multiply, not an RL workload. Its figure was 4.49 ms ± 79.9 μs per loop on CPU.

For RL specifically, you'd likely need to benchmark environment stepping and the policy update on your own machine. Small, sequential RL workloads often run best on CPU, and the GPU backends above are immature and have coverage gaps.

If the metric rewards consistency, self-consistency voting and deterministic decoding matter more than a bigger model.\n\n## Track 4: LLM agents for high-frequency trading\n\n### Where the field is\n\n- Most LLM trading results do not survive careful testing. FINSABER re-ran published LLM strategies over 20 years with bias controls: the edge mostly vanishes. LLM strategies are too cautious in bull markets and lose heavily in bear markets.\n- Memorisation is a real leak. LLMs recall exact pre-cutoff prices and macro figures, and telling them to ignore the future does not work. Any backtest inside the model's training window is suspect. Fixes in the literature: anonymise tickers (BlindTrade), test only after the cutoff, or measure contamination (MemGuard-Alpha).\n- TradingAgents (multi-agent desk: analysts, debaters, trader, risk manager) is the most starred framework; its headline results rest on a few months of data and its buy-and-hold baseline has been disputed.\n- Live arenas: Nof1's Alpha Arena Season 1 (Oct to Nov 2025, real money, crypto perps) left four of six frontier models in loss. ## Track 3: voice agents on ServiceNow
- **ServiceNow publishes its own benchmarks.** [EnterpriseOps-Gym](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.13594) has 1,150 text tasks, scored on the final database state; the best model gets about 34%. [EVA-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13841) has 213 voice scenarios with an accuracy score and an experience score; no system gets above 0.5 on both.
- **Voice loses most of what text agents can do.** In [τ-Voice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.13686), GPT-5 solves 85% of tasks in text but voice agents get 26 to 51%. Consistency across repeated attempts is the 2026 theme, more than peak scores.
- **Pipelines still win on accuracy.** Speech-to-text, then an LLM, then text-to-speech still beats speech-to-speech models on accuracy, even with open full-duplex models like NVIDIA's [VoiceChat](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/166988).
- **On the M1:** Parakeet through MLX or Core ML for speech recognition ([speed test](https://github.com/anvanvan/mac-whisper-speedtest)), [Smart Turn v3](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/smart-turn) to detect when the speaker has finished, and small LLMs through MLX. The open speech models need Kaggle GPUs.

## Track 4: LLM agents for HFT
- **Most LLM trading gains don't survive careful testing.** [FINSABER](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.07078v2) re-ran published strategies over 20 years and the advantage mostly vanished.
- **Memorisation inflates backtests.** LLMs remember prices from before their training cutoff ([The Memorization Problem](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.14765v2)).
- **Live trading went badly.** In [Alpha Arena](https://forklog.com/en/four-out-of-six-ai-models-suffer-losses-in-trading-tournament/) Season 1, four of six models lost real money.
- **Speed is the binding limit.** [HFTBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19481) shows a faster, smaller model can beat a better, slower one. The credible design: the LLM runs a slow loop that writes alpha factors ([AlphaForgeBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18481v1)), and a fast model executes.
- **Baselines to beat:** DeepLOB, [LOBCAST](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.01915v1) (every model it tests drops sharply on new data) and Kronos.
- **Likely Kaggle shape:** Optiver or Jane Street style. That means gradient-boosted trees on order-book features, time-ordered CV with purging, and online updating where the data allows.

## Track 5: safe RL tuning for MASA
- **[MASA-Safe-RL](https://github.com/sacktock/MASA-Safe-RL)** is Imperial FMAI Lab's library. It has tabular and PPO, TRPO and CPO variants (some with Lagrangian penalties), plus shielding. Settings live in YAML files, it runs on JAX, and it already has a `masa benchmark` command.
- **[Issue #141](https://github.com/sacktock/MASA-Safe-RL/issues/141) is effectively the track brief:** "possibly with raytune", with results in a `MASA-Zoo` repo. That repo doesn't exist yet, so nobody has started this.
- **What the literature says:**
  - Tune on different seeds from the ones you test on ([Eimer et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.01324)).
  - Use [ARLBench](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.18827v2) as a template.
  - Report with [rliable](https://research.google/blog/rliable-towards-reliable-evaluation-reporting-in-reinforcement-learning/): interquartile mean with bootstrap confidence intervals.
  - Lagrangian methods are fragile ([comparison](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.17564v2)), so their multiplier settings are what to tune.
  - Safe RL has two objectives, return and cost. Ray Tune handles both through Optuna; its early-stopping scheduler (ASHA) can't.
- **On the M1:** JAX on CPU. Apple's Metal backend for JAX is effectively abandoned.

Adversarial validation is a standard Kaggle diagnostic for checking whether your validation split resembles the test data. The core idea is to train a classifier to tell training rows from test rows. The sources agree on the basics, with some differences in emphasis.

- **Method:** One source describes it as a binary classification task: drop the training target, label training rows 0 and test rows 1, merge and shuffle, then train a classifier and record the metric. Another proposes a variant that selects the training examples most similar to the test examples and uses them as a validation set.
- **Interpreting the score:** The metric is typically ROC AUC. If the data share one distribution, a classifier should do no better than chance, which corresponds to a ROC AUC of 0.5. A score well above 0.5 signals a shift, so the current validation strategy may produce overly optimistic estimates of model performance.
- **Diagnosing the cause:** The fitted model can point to the culprit. You can analyze the learned model to diagnose the problem, and once you understand it, you can work on fixing it. The Kaggle Book discusses identifying the features responsible for the shift and redesigning the validation process to better match the target distribution.
- **Real example:** One source notes that this happens in the Santander Customer Satisfaction competition at Kaggle.
- **Tooling:** The open-source `advertion` package wraps the workflow in a single `validate` call and reports whether the datasets follow the same distribution, along with the mean ROC AUC and the adversarial features. Its example output reports a mean ROC AUC of about 0.502 and flags the 'id' feature as adversarial.

**Competition:** March 2026 Kaggle Playground churn prediction (Series S6E3), scored by AUC.

**How LLM agents were used**
- Three LLM agents (GPT-5.4 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Claude Opus 4.6) worked within a "human-in-the-loop workflow."
- The agents followed a guided sequence from the author's earlier Kaggle Grandmaster playbook: EDA, baselines, feature engineering, then model combination.
- Agents wrote over 600,000 lines of code and ran 850 experiments.
- GPU libraries (cuDF, cuML, GPU gradient-boosted trees, and PyTorch) ran each experiment quickly.

**Workflow steps**
1. **EDA:** Agents examined row/column counts, the target, feature types, and missing data, either through prompts or by running code themselves.
2. **Baselines:** Agents wrote k-fold pipelines (e.g., XGBoost) that saved out-of-fold (OOF) and test predictions for every model.
3. **Feature engineering and tuning:** Agents iterated on new ideas, keeping any change that improved CV and saving predictions for every experiment, good or bad.
4. **Combination:** Agents summarized experiments, merged ideas into stronger single models, used knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling, and built ensembles through hill climbing and stacking with ridge/logistic, NN, and GBDT meta-models.

**Human vs. agent roles**
- *Human:* Designed the workflow, wrote the prompts, ran code where agents couldn't, chose which ideas to pursue, and brainstormed with the LLMs.
- *Agents:* Wrote and debugged code, generated and tested feature ideas, summarized results, and built the ensembles.

The article doesn't spell out the exact division of labor beyond this.

**Final solution**
- A four-level stack of 150 models, selected from the 850 experiments.
- Per the figure description, level one extracts features, levels two and three extract patterns, and level four predicts the target.

**Time taken:** The article doesn't say how long the project took.

**Key lessons**
- Fast code generation plus fast execution shortens the experiment loop, which is the main benefit.
- Saving OOF and test predictions for every experiment makes later ensembling and stacking possible.
- Diverse models and features matter, and it helps to have agents summarize results across many experiments.
- The approach is meant for any tabular prediction task, not just Kaggle.
```

**Tool result**

```
**Foundations:** Run fast experiments by GPU-accelerating dataframes and models. Use k-fold CV that matches the test structure, such as TimeSeriesSplit for time-dependent data or GroupKFold for grouped data.

1. **Smarter EDA:** Go beyond missing values and correlations. Compare train and test feature distributions to catch shift, and plot the target over time to check for trends and seasonality. cuDF makes these comparisons fast on large data.

2. **Diverse baselines:** Build linear, gradient-boosted tree, and small neural net baselines early. Compare them side by side to see which model family fits your data best. Re-run them after data changes to catch problems like leakage.

3. **Feature generation:** Create hundreds or thousands of features rather than a handful. For example, combine pairs of categorical columns into interaction features (eight columns yielded 28 new pairs). cuDF speeds up groupby, aggregation, and encoding.

4. **Hill climbing:** Start with your best single model, then add others with blend weights. Keep only the additions that improve validation, and repeat until gains stop. Vectorizing metrics with CuPy lets you test many weight combinations in parallel.

5. **Stacking:** Train a second-level model on first-level outputs. Use residual stacking, where Stage 2 predicts Stage 1's errors, or OOF stacking, where Stage 1 predictions become Stage 2 features. cuML and GPU boosted trees make deep, multi-level stacks practical.

6. **Pseudo-labeling:** Use your strongest model (ideally an ensemble) to label test or external data, then add those labels to training. Use soft labels (probabilities), try multiple rounds, and filter low-confidence samples. Under k-fold, generate k sets of pseudo-labels so validation folds never see labels from models trained on them.

7. **Extra training:** Average predictions across many random seeds, since ensembling 100 XGBoost seeds outperformed single-seed training in the article's example. After tuning hyperparameters, retrain the final model on 100% of the data.
```

## Claude (2026-10-24 01:11:49 UTC)

I read about 13 sources and saved the result to memory as a 12-step playbook. It's the default order for any Kaggle task we do.

**Short version:**
1. **Validation before anything else.** The folds must copy how the test set was split. Make 2 or 3 early submissions to check that local CV moves with the public leaderboard. If it does, trust CV from then on. The public leaderboard is a small, noisy sample, and repeatedly testing against it overfits it ([the Ladder](https://www.arxiv-vanity.com/papers/1502.04585/)). Teams that chased it have dropped hundreds of places at the final reveal ([essay-scoring example](https://datancoffee.substack.com/p/the-scandal-at-kaggle)).
2. **Adversarial validation on day one.** Train a model to tell train rows from test rows. If it can't (a score near 0.5), the two match. If it can, find the features that differ ([KDnuggets](https://www.kdnuggets.com/2020/02/adversarial-validation-overview.html)).
3. **Speed of experiments matters most.** Change one thing at a time and keep it only if CV improves. Save the out-of-fold and test predictions from every experiment, including the bad ones; they're the raw material for ensembling ([NVIDIA playbook](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/the-kaggle-grandmasters-playbook-7-battle-tested-modeling-techniques-for-tabular-data)).
4. **Try several model families early:** linear, gradient-boosted trees and a small neural net. Tabular competitions are still mostly won by gradient-boosted trees, image ones by CNNs with augmentation, text ones by transformers ([Kaggle Chronicles](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.06304), [mlcontests analysis](https://forums.fast.ai/t/analysis-of-83-ml-competitions-in-2021/93844)).
5. **Ensemble last:**
   - Blend greedily: add a model with a weight only while CV improves.
   - Then train a simple second-level model on the saved predictions.
   - Optionally label the test set with your best model's probabilities, done fold by fold so no fold sees its own labels.
   - Average many random seeds and retrain on all the data.
6. **Design for the metric and study the failures.** Across 80 medical-imaging challenges, winners used augmentation 100% of the time and post-processing 66% ([Why is the Winner the Best?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17719)).
7. **Using AI well:** the best agent on [MLE-bench](https://openai.com/index/mle-bench/) earned a medal in only about 17% of 75 competitions. [AIDE](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.13138) works best by making small, focused changes and fixing rather than restarting. NVIDIA [won a March 2026 competition](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/winning-a-kaggle-competition-with-generative-ai-assisted-coding/) with three LLM agents running 850 experiments. A human designed the workflow and chose which ideas to pursue, so that's the split I'd suggest for us.
8. **Final two picks:** the best robust CV score, plus a hedge that's genuinely different.

## Claude (2026-10-24 01:14:32 UTC)

Yes, understood, and I've saved it to memory. Whatever track we take, we run many agents in parallel and aim as high as we can.

**How we'll run it:**
1. **Lock the foundations first, one agent only (about the first hour).** That means the CV folds saved to a file, the metric code, adversarial validation and a LightGBM baseline. Nothing runs in parallel until these are frozen. If agents start from different folds, their CV scores can't be compared and the ensemble leaks.
2. **Then fan out.** Each agent owns one wayfinder ticket (a feature family, model family, pretrained model or external dataset) in its own worktree. All agents read the same folds and save their out-of-fold and test predictions, plus a log entry, to a shared registry.
3. **A checker agent re-runs every claimed CV gain and looks for leakage before it's merged.** This works like Athena in paladin: nothing goes in on an agent's word alone.
4. **An ensembler agent keeps blending and stacking over the registry** as new predictions arrive.
5. **You choose direction and the final 2 submissions; I orchestrate.** That's the split that won NVIDIA's competition.

**The real limits are not code or complexity:**
- **Compute.** The M1 plus your Kaggle GPU quota decide how many experiments can actually run at once. Tree models on CPU parallelise well; GPU work will queue on Kaggle.
- **Daily submission limit.** That's fine, since we trust CV, not the leaderboard.
- **The organisers' re-run and walkthrough call.** However ambitious the solution, it must rebuild from one reproducible notebook, and you must be able to explain every part of it. I'll keep a write-up as we go so the call is easy.

The default for a workflow is under 5 agents. Your instruction overrides that, so I'll scale to what the hardware can feed.

Send the task when it drops at 10:00 and I'll start step 1 immediately.

## Claude (2026-10-24 09:04:55 UTC)

I've read all of it and updated memory with the task and the new rules.

## Rules that change how we work
- **Train on Kaggle only.** The M1 becomes the place where code is written and agents are coordinated. Every experiment runs as a Kaggle notebook, sent from here with the Kaggle command-line tool. So the number of agents running at once is capped by how many notebooks Kaggle runs at once and by your GPU quota.
- **Every AI chat must be exported, or you're disqualified.** I'll keep a list of every session and agent we use and export them all at the end. The judges also score "good use of AI", so how we work is part of the mark.
- **No forking public notebooks.** We write from scratch and cite anything we read.
- **Half the score is the public leaderboard, not the private one.** CV still drives decisions, but the public number is what gets marked, so I'll plan every submission against the daily limit.
- **The report's structure matches our experiment log.** Hypotheses, an ablation table and one failure come straight out of it.

## First read of the task
- **The data looks structured.** 2,699 passages is almost exactly 150 prompts × 18 models, so each prompt was probably answered once by every model. The test set of about 4,000 is about 222 × 18. If EDA confirms this:
  1. **CV must group folds by prompt (GroupKFold).** Otherwise passages on the same topic sit on both sides of a fold and CV looks better than it is.
  2. **This is the biggest lever I can see.** Within a prompt, each model appears exactly once. We cluster test passages by prompt (they share a topic), then make each cluster's labels a strict one-to-one match on the predicted probabilities. That could lift a 0.6 classifier a long way, and we can measure the gain honestly in CV first. It's an algorithm, not hand-labelling, but I'd confirm it's allowed through the private ticket channel. Asking in kaggle-help would give the idea away.
- **Most errors will probably be between models from the same lab.** Predicting the lab first, then the model, may help.
- **The plan, from simple to ambitious:**
  1. Character and word n-grams plus style features (formatting, punctuation, unusual characters).
  2. Embeddings from a frozen LLM with a simple classifier on top.
  3. Fine-tuning DeBERTa or ModernBERT.
  4. LoRA fine-tuning of 7 to 14B LLMs as classifiers.
  5. Public external data labelled by model, if the versions and licences fit.
  6. Pseudo-labelling the 4,000 test passages.
  7. Ensemble, then the one-to-one matching.
- **The 9-hour offline inference limit is generous.** 4,000 short passages fit several 8B models easily.

Overview
Ask 18 frontier language models the same question, and no two answers read quite the same. Even in a single short paragraph, every model leaves subtle clues in its word choice, tone, and sentence structure.

In this competition, you'll identify which among 18 leading models wrote each unlabeled passage. Your work will sharpen methods for AI provenance and benchmark auditing.

10 days ago

Merger & Entry
Description
18 large language models from six AI labs now generate everything from code explanations to creative fiction. As model-generated text fills the web and training datasets, knowing which model wrote a given passage is critical for auditing synthetic data and detecting benchmark contamination. Yet telling frontier models apart from a single short paragraph remains surprisingly difficult.

Standard AI detectors only try to separate machine-written text from human writing. Pinpointing the exact source model (a task known as authorship attribution) is much harder when prompts are unseen and passage lengths vary randomly between 40 and 250 words. You can't rely on simple character-count shortcuts or topic keywords. However, each lab's training data and post-training choices leave behind distinct stylistic fingerprints in vocabulary, phrasing, and punctuation.

In this competition, hosted by Kaggle, you'll build models to classify ~4,000 unlabeled text passages across 18 frontier language models from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Qwen, ZAI, and Moonshot AI. Every passage in the dataset is an authentic, self-contained response to prompts covering philosophy, physics, mathematics, biology, computer science, and creative prose.

Your solutions will show how reliably today's frontier models can be fingerprinted from short text alone. Better attribution methods will help researchers audit open benchmarks and understand what makes each model family distinct.

Timeline

January 6, 2027 - Entry Deadline. You must accept the competition rules before this date in order to compete.

All deadlines are at 11:59 PM UTC on the corresponding day unless otherwise noted. The competition organizers reserve the right to update the contest timeline if they deem it necessary.

Evaluation
Submissions are evaluated on balanced accuracy: the average, over all candidate models, of the fraction of that model's test passages you labelled correctly (per-class recall).

sample_submission.parquet

## Claude (2026-10-24 09:06:20 UTC)

I've read it and added it to memory. Here's what changes.

**Facts that shape the plan:**
- **Train has `prompt_id`; test doesn't.** So GroupKFold by `prompt_id` is our CV, and it matches the "unseen prompts" test exactly.
- **Test counts per model are unequal, and the public and private leaderboards have different model mixes.** That breaks my strict one-to-one matching idea, since a prompt doesn't always have exactly one passage per model. A weaker version may survive. If train shows a model **never appears twice for the same prompt**, we can still match passages to models with "at most once each" inside each prompt cluster. EDA will check this and CV will measure what it's worth before we rely on it.
- **Balanced accuracy with uneven test counts** means we keep the model's probabilities neutral, treating every model as equally likely, and don't let it favour common models. Every model counts the same.
- **14 of the 18 labels come from three labs:** 5 OpenAI, 4 Google, 5 Anthropic. Telling the lab apart is probably the easy part. Separating close relatives (the three gpt-5.6 variants, the flash models, the Opus versions) will decide the ranking.
- **The competition has been public for 10 days.** There are public notebooks and discussions behind the ~0.70 leader. We can read them and cite them, but never fork them.
- **Some formatting survives.** Only "light formatting cleanup" was applied, so punctuation and character-level fingerprints are still there.
- **The notebook contract:** read `/kaggle/input/competitions/name-that-llm/test.csv` and write `submission.parquet` (id, model). The notebook must run offline within 9 hours on CPU or GPU, and the interactive session only shows a few example test rows.

- **Existing public datasets with these exact model versions.** They're unlikely to exist, but I'll check.

Yet, despite their solid appearance, these buried salt giants are far from static. Under the immense lithostatic pressure of the overburden, the salt becomes highly ductile. Yielding to gravity and compressive forces, the evaporites deform and mobilize, flowing upward through the crust like slow glaciers to create towering diapirs, intricate canopies, and sweeping salt domes that continuously reshape the deep landscape.'}]

Breaking one can disqualify the entry.\n\n- **Train on Kaggle only.** Every model fit runs in a Kaggle notebook under the account `nabilshah`. The local machine is for writing code, orchestrating runs and descriptive EDA.\n- **No forking public notebooks.** Start from the official starter or from scratch. Public work may be read; cite it in `CITATIONS.md`.\n- **Free and public only.** External data and pretrained models must be free and publicly available. Each one is listed in `CITATIONS.md`. No paid APIs.\n- **Every AI session is logged.** Each Claude Code session, subagent run, workflow or other AI chat gets a row in `docs/ai-sessions.md` and is exported before submission. Missing logs mean disqualification.\n- **Folds are frozen.** Cross-validation is `GroupKFold` on `prompt_id`, fixed in phase 0. Every experiment uses the same folds file. Changing it needs an ADR.\n- **Every experiment is logged.** It saves out-of-fold and test predictions and adds a row to `docs/experiments/LOG.md`: the change, local CV against the baseline, and the next step.\n- **Seeds are fixed** in every notebook and script.\n- **The repository stays private** until after the deadline. No code or ideas are shared with other participants.\n\n## Phases\n\nWork is organised into phases. Each phase maps to one milestone (`vX.Y.Z`) and one `phase-N` label. A phase ends when its milestone closes. `ROADMAP.md` holds the live phase table.\n\n## Tracks\n\nIf the work splits into parallel workstreams, each gets a `track-*` label (for example `track-a`, `track-b`). Not in use until that happens.\n\n## The wayfinder protocol\n\nEach phase opens with one `wayfinder:map` issue: the phase's single source of truth for what's known, decided, and next.\n\nA map issue body has three sections, kept up to date as children close:\n\n- **Fog**: open unknowns.\n- **Decisions so far**: what's been settled, and why.\n- **Frontier**: the next unblocked tickets.\n\nChild tickets hang off the map issue with a `Part of: #n` line, and carry one of:\n\n- `wayfinder:research`: investigate and report back, no implementation.\n- `wayfinder:grilling`: stress-test a plan or decision before committing to it.\n- `wayfinder:prototype`: throwaway build to answer a design question.\n- `wayfinder:task`: a concrete, scoped piece of work. For this repository, usually one experiment.\n\n## Labels\n\n- Phase: `phase-0`, `phase-1`, and so on.\n- Track: `track-a`, `track-b`, added once more than one workstream exists.\n- Wayfinder: `wayfinder:map`, `wayfinder:research`, `wayfinder:grilling`, `wayfinder:prototype`, `wayfinder:task`.\n- Severity: `p1`, `p2`, `p3`.\n- Workflow: `needs-decision`, `needs-research`, `needs-repro`, `ready-for-agent`.\n- Defaults: `bug`, `documentation`, `enhancement`.\n\n## Research\n\nOutput of a `wayfinder:research` ticket lands in `docs/research/issue-<n>-<slug>.md`. Every file ends with a recommendation. A recommendation that's adopted gets promoted to a numbered ADR in `docs/adr/`.\n\n## Architecture decisions\n\n`docs/adr/` holds numbered ADRs, one decision per file, starting from `docs/adr/0000-template.md`. The index lives in `docs/adr/README.md` and must stay in sync with the files present.\n\n## Layout\n\n- `notebooks/`: one folder per Kaggle notebook, each with its `kernel-metadata.json`.\n- `src/`: shared code (folds, metric, features) used by the notebooks.\n- `docs/experiments/LOG.md`: the experiment log, one row per run.\n- `docs/ai-sessions.md`: every AI session used, for export at the end.\n- `CITATIONS.md`: every public notebook, dataset and pretrained model used.\n- `data/`, `outputs/`: local only, gitignored.\n\n## Pull requests\n\n- Title: Conventional Commits, with scope where it helps, for example `feat(features): add char n-gram tf-idf (#12)`.\n- Body: *What this does*, *Why*, a checklist, and a test plan. For an experiment, include the CV result and the log row.\n- Reference the issue with `refs #n`, not `closes #n`. The maintainer closes issues on merge.\n- Small commits, Conventional Commits, no co-author trailers.\n\n## House style\n\n- British English throughout.\n- No em dashes.\n- Short and direct. No filler, no hedging.\n\n## Documents\n\nReference materials go in `/materials/`, which is gitignored and never committed.\n"

## Claude (2026-10-24 10:17:42 UTC)

The private repo is set up and the read-only EDA is done. I didn't fit any model locally, only counted things.

## What the data says
1. **The structure is confirmed.** There are 2,699 rows, 150 per model (claude-fable-5 has 149), with no nulls or duplicates. Every prompt has **exactly one passage per model**: 149 prompts have all 18, and `p002` is missing claude-fable-5. So GroupKFold on `prompt_id` is the right CV, and "at most one passage per model per prompt" holds in train.
2. **The matching idea looks workable.** Passages for the same prompt often share an opening phrase; for one prompt, 5 of the 18 start "When a language dies". Clustering test passages back into prompts should be easy. Because test counts per model are uneven, the matching has to allow a model to be missing from a prompt, not force exactly one of each.
3. **Length is noise.** Every passage is a single paragraph with no markdown. Length varies as much within a prompt as across the whole set (spread of 57.8 words within a prompt against 58.3 overall), so it says nothing about the model.
4. **Punctuation separates the labs:**

| Lab | Em dashes | Curly quotes | Straight apostrophes | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude | 63–83% of passages | never | ~60% | |
| GLM | 63–83% of passages | never | ~60% | expect it to be confused with Claude |
| Gemini | none at all | some | some | |
| GPT | 9–37% | ~50% | almost never in the gpt-5.6 models | |
| Kimi | 52% | 37% | 23% | mixes both styles |
| Qwen | 3% | 29% | | most commas (11.8 per 100 words) |

5. **Vocabulary carries fingerprints too:**
   - Gemini writes ornate prose: profound, expanse, intricate, primordial, abyss.
   - GPT-5.6 hedges with may, can, therefore.
   - claude-fable-5 tells stories: she, her, told.
   - Kimi: patience, keeps, becomes. Qwen: luminous, turning, becoming.
6. **The hard part is models from the same lab.** The three gpt-5.6 models, the three Gemini flash models and the Opus versions have identical punctuation, so separating them depends on word choice and meaning. That's where fine-tuned LLMs need to earn their place.
7. **Accented and special characters are weak.** They mostly come from names like Gödel and Schrödinger. The Unicode minus sign appears mostly in GPT text.

## Repo
[Nabzx/name-that-llm](https://github.com/Nabzx/name-that-llm) is private and has 12 small Conventional Commits with no trailers. It contains:
- `AGENTS.md`, with the competition rules written in as invariants (train on Kaggle only, no forking, every AI session logged, frozen folds).
- `CLAUDE.md`, a roadmap with phases 0 to 5, and the wayfinder issue and PR templates.
- Empty ADR, research, experiment log, AI sessions and citations files.
- The phase labels and milestones on GitHub.

I moved my track research into the gitignored `materials/` folder, and the downloaded data is gitignored too.

**Left for you to write:** the map issue for each phase, the research notes, and the rows in the AI sessions file. This session should be row 1 there.

**Kaggle limits:** 5 submissions a day, 30 GPU hours and 20 TPU hours, which reset on 31 Oct.

## Suggested first tickets for Phase 0 (for you to write)
- **task:** freeze the 5 GroupKFold folds on `prompt_id`, plus the balanced accuracy metric.
- **task:** a baseline notebook using character and word n-gram TF-IDF with logistic regression, then a first submission to check that CV and the leaderboard move together.
- **prototype:** cluster test passages back into prompts and apply the matching, with the gain measured in CV.
- **research:** read the public notebooks and discussions, and cite them.
- **grilling:** is the matching within the rules? This is a question for the organisers through the private ticket channel.

Once the folds and baseline tickets exist, I'll build both and push them to Kaggle.

[MD] # Two-stage LoRA on the public pool (LB 0.592)

**The problem in one line.** Telling Claude from GPT is easy. Telling `gemini 3.7 flash` from `gemini 3.8 flash` is the whole game, and the host gives us only 150 passages per model to learn it from.

**The idea.** Other Kagglers have published about 35,000 passages from these same 18 models, written to prompts in the competition's style. That is 13 times the training set. So we teach in two stages, the way you'd learn a language:

1. **Read a lot first.** Train a LoRA classifier on the public passages only. It learns what each model *sounds like*.
2. **Then listen to the teacher.** Fine tune it for 2 epochs on the host's 2,699 passages. It learns how each model sounded *when the host asked*: same settings, same formatting.

Stage 1 alone already matches a LoRA trained on the host data. Stage 2 adds another 9 points.

| Model | Local CV (5-fold, grouped by prompt) | Public LB |
|---|---|---|
| n-gram SVC on train + pool | 0.435 | |
| Qwen3-8B LoRA, public passages only (stage 1) | 0.483 | |
| Qwen3-8B LoRA, stage 1 + stage 2 | 0.569 | |
| Qwen3-14B LoRA, stage 1 + stage 2 | 0.569 | |
| **This notebook:** 8B + 14B + n-gram, centred twin, balancing | **0.593** | **0.592** |

The two LoRAs score the same alone but disagree on 22% of passages, which is why blending them helps.

**What runs here** (inference only, about 1 h on 2x T4 for the full test):
1. An n-gram model, fit here on train + pool.
2. Two LoRA checkpoints (Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B), trained offline. The training recipe is at the end.
3. A "centred twin" that compares passages answering the same question.
4. A log-probability blend, then class balancing.

[MD] ## 1. The n gram model

Each model has typing habits. In the training data claude and GLM never use curly quotes, while gpt uses a curly apostrophe in about half its passages. Gemini almost never uses an em dash, while Claude uses one in three passages out of four. Character n grams pick this up.

We look at each passage four ways: raw characters +  words plus punctuation +  the *shape* of the text (`Xxxx xx x`) + function words only, with every content word replaced by `CONTENT` so the topic can't leak in. A linear SVM sits on top, trained on train + the public pool with balanced class weights.

[MD] ## 2. The LoRA classifiers

Each checkpoint is a LoRA adapter on the **first 24 layers of Qwen3 8B** (or the first 27 of Qwen3 14B). We don't need the rest: style lives in the early and middle layers, while the last layers mostly encode the topic, which is useless here because test prompts are new.

For each passage we:
1. merge the adapter into the weights once (`W <- W + B A * alpha / r`), so no `peft` is needed
2. run the passage and take the mean hidden state at 8 depths (layers 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24), each through its own LayerNorm;
3. concatenate them (8 x 4096 numbers) and apply a linear layer to get 18 score

[MD] ## How the checkpoints were trained

Both checkpoints use the same recipe. It is the public "LoRA24" recipe with one change: a first stage on public data.

- **Model:** Qwen3-8B-Base (first 24 layers) or Qwen3-14B-Base (first 27 layers), LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05 on every linear layer, 8 pooled layers with a LayerNorm each, two linear heads (plain and centred).
- **Batches:** triplets of passages that answer the same prompt, 6 triplets per step. The loss is the cross-entropy of the plain head plus the cross-entropy of the centred head on triplet-centred features, which teaches the model to tell apart answers to *the same* question.
- **Stage 1:** 1 epoch over the 34,940 public passages, class-weighted cross-entropy (the pool is unbalanced), AdamW lr 1e-4 (LoRA) / 1e-3 (heads), 10% warm-up then cosine.
- **Stage 2:** 2 epochs on the host's 2,699 passages, lr 5e-5 / 5e-4. More epochs over-fit, and mixing pool passages back in made it worse.
- Trained in bf16 on one RTX 5090: about 30 min (8B) and 90 min (14B) per checkpoint.

**The pool** merges 14 public datasets, keeping single-paragraph passages of 30-300 words with no markdown. Exact duplicates and anything identical to a training passage are dropped. One more filter: if a model *never* shows a mark in the training data (an em dash for Gemini, curly quotes for Claude), its pool passages containing that mark are dropped. That leaves 34,940 passages for all 18 models (1,100-2,700 per model).

**What did not help**, so you can skip it: a larger backbone on its own (14B = 8B at 0.569), seed averaging, extra family "gates" on top of the blend, Hungarian assignment inside topic clusters, and more epochs in stage 2.

**Paper:** "Who's Behind the Text? Robust Model Authorship Attribution" (arXiv:2610.19583, cs.AI), by Minseok Ko, Hyunseok Lee, Woomin Song, Beomjun Kim, Jinwoo Shin, and Kunwoong Kim. Submitted 14 October 2026.

**Method:** The authors propose ATLAS (Authorship Tracing via Likelihood-based Attribution of Sources). It treats attribution as "source-conditioned text modeling rather than direct source prediction." It learns how text from each source family is generated, then assigns a text to the source whose learned condition gives it the highest likelihood. Token-level likelihood evidence is aggregated with clipping so that no single token dominates the decision. The page does not say whether this is exactly a token-likelihood ratio, so that detail is unconfirmed.

**Training, models, and datasets:** The page does not describe the training procedure, the specific LLMs involved, or the training data. It names two benchmarks: MAABench, which the authors introduce to test out-of-distribution settings such as domain and model version shifts, and OpenTuringBench.

**Headline results:**
- On MAABench, when both the generation domain and model version change, ATLAS reaches 74.27% accuracy, 9.00 percentage points above the strongest baseline.
- ATLAS outperforms existing baselines on both MAABench and OpenTuringBench.
- Beyond attribution, ATLAS can identify distillation sources by finding which source model a target LLM most closely resembles. The authors report that it recovers the known teacher of every distilled model they evaluated.

**Provider vs. model-level accuracy:** The page does not report any finding on this distinction.

The paper is arXiv 2502.12150, "Idiosyncrasies in Large Language Models" by Mingjie Sun, Yida Yin, Zhiqiu Xu, J. Zico Kolter, and Zhuang Liu. It was published at ICML 2025.

- **Task:** The authors frame a synthetic task in which a model must identify which LLM produced a given text. Given a particular text output, the objective is to predict the source LLM that generates the text.
- **Method and result:** Fine-tuning text embedding models on LLM outputs works well for this. They reach 97.1% accuracy on held-out validation data in the five-way classification problem involving ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini, and DeepSeek.
- **Source of the signal:** The idiosyncrasies are rooted in word-level distributions. The authors also report that these patterns persist even when the texts are rewritten, translated, or summarized by an external LLM, which suggests they are also present in the semantic content.
- **Further work:** The authors use LLMs as judges to produce open-ended descriptions of each model's idiosyncrasies. They also discuss implications for training on synthetic data, inferring model similarity, and robust evaluation of LLMs.

A third-party review site summarizes the paper's qualitative findings, including differences in formatting habits. I did not check those claims against the paper itself, so rely on the arXiv or ICML versions for details. The code is linked from the arXiv abstract page.

## Claude (2026-10-24 10:35:32 UTC)

Understood. I'll stop creating docs and give you the directions here.

## What I found
- **Scores to beat.** The public leaderboard top is **0.700**. The best public notebook scores **0.639**, and it's built almost entirely from other people's published model weights.
- **The recipe that works:**
  - Train first on a public "in-style" pool of 76–84k passages. Other participants generated it and released it free across 26 datasets, mostly under an open licence that only asks for credit (CC BY 4.0).
  - Fine-tune the same model on the host's 2,699 passages.
  - The best single model is a LoRA on the first 27 layers of Qwen3-14B Base, at **0.611** CV. A word-and-character n-gram SVC scores 0.473 and DeBERTa-v3-large scores 0.546.
  - Blend them, then rebalance so every model gets equal probability mass (Sinkhorn balancing).
- **What doesn't work.** My one-to-one matching idea is dead: the hidden test has only 1–5 passages per prompt, so hard matching raises CV but lowers the leaderboard. Soft prompt-centring only adds about 0.005. Gates for single families, more epochs and seed averaging didn't help either.
- **The hardest pairs** are glm-5.3 against glm-5.3-flash and gemini-3.7-flash against 3.8-flash. Every public model gets stuck there.
- **CV overstates the leaderboard** by 0.02–0.04 for models trained on the pool.
- **Compute is our real limit.** The public models were trained on an RTX 5090 (90 minutes per 14B checkpoint). Our T4s are several times slower, so a full 14B with 5 folds won't fit in 30 GPU hours. An 8B will.
- **My clustering check on train:** grouping passages by topic recovers about half the same-prompt pairs with almost no wrong merges.

## Three directions

**1. Build the winning recipe ourselves.** We make our own pool from the public datasets and train our own two-stage LoRA (Qwen3-8B on the T4s), SVC and DeBERTa, then blend and balance.
- Expected leaderboard: about 0.58–0.61. Uses most of the GPU budget.
- Every weight is ours, so it's the cleanest story for the report and call.
- The ceiling sits below people who reuse published weights.

**2. Start from published weights and push past them.** We load the public checkpoints in our own notebook (cited, not forked) to reach about 0.62–0.64 within hours. Then we spend our GPU on what's missing: specialists for the two hardest pairs, plus a new backbone such as Gemma 4 or Llama 3.1 for diversity.
- Expected leaderboard: about 0.64–0.67. This is the highest leaderboard ceiling, and that's half the score.
- Judges may see the base as other people's work, so our additions must be clearly ours.
- The rules allow public pretrained models, but this is the grey edge of them.

**3. Lab witnesses (new idea).** We run every passage through one open model per lab and score it: gpt-oss-20b (OpenAI), Gemma 4 (Google), Qwen3, GLM-4 (ZAI) and Moonlight-16B (Moonshot). How likely each model finds every word becomes a set of features for a small classifier. The idea is that a lab's open model knows its siblings' habits. It's backed by [ATLAS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19583), which attributes text by likelihood, and [Idiosyncrasies in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12150).
- Expected: about 0.45–0.55 alone, or +0.01–0.03 added to a blend. Cheap to train.
- Strongest novelty and the best report story. It also ties to tracks 3 and 4.
- It's unproven, and Claude has no open model to act as its witness.

**My recommendation:** 2 as the spine, with 3 as our own contribution. That gets a leaderboard score that competes with anyone stacking public weights, plus something original to show in the report and call. If you want every weight to be ours, take 1 + 3, accepting a lower leaderboard score.

## Questions
1. **Pushing notebooks to Kaggle:** training must happen on Kaggle, so I need to push notebooks to Kaggle to run them. That isn't a competition submission. Is it OK?
2. **Published weights:** are you comfortable using other participants' published weights? This decides 1 versus 2. We could also ask the organisers privately first.
3. **The GitHub tickets:** #2 to #6 are already open. Shall I close them as superseded, or keep them and post these findings as comments?

tool results are cut in the Markdown only, never in the raw file\n\n\ndef find_transcript(session_id):\n    hits = list(PROJECTS.glob(f\"*/{session_id}.jsonl\"))\n    assert len(hits) == 1, f\"expected one transcript for {session_id}, found {hits}\"\n    return hits[0]\n\n\ndef render(jsonl):\n    out = []\n    for line in jsonl.open():\n        entry = json.loads(line)\n        kind = entry.get(\"type\")\n        if kind not in (\"user\", \"assistant\"):\n            continue\n        content = entry.get(\"message\", {}).get(\"content\")\n        stamp = entry.get(\"timestamp\", \"\")[:19].replace(\"T\", \" \")\n        if isinstance(content, str):\n            out.append(f\"## {'Nabil' if kind == 'user' else 'Claude'} ({stamp} UTC)\\n\\n{content}\\n\")\n            continue\n        for block in content or []:\n            t = block.get(\"type\")\n            if t == \"text\" and block.get(\"text\", \"\").strip():\n                who = \"Nabil\" if kind == \"user\" else \"Claude\"\n                out.append(f\"## {who} ({stamp} UTC)\\n\\n{block['text']}\\n\")\n            elif t == \"tool_use\":\n                args = json.dumps(block.get(\"input\", {}), indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)\n                out.append(f\"**Tool call: {block.get('name')}**\\n\\n```json\\n{args}\\n```\\n\")\n            elif t == \"tool_result\":\n                body = block.get(\"content\")\n                if isinstance(body, list):\n                    body = \"\\n\".join(b.get(\"text\", \"\") for b in body if isinstance(b, dict))\n                body = str(body or \"\")\n                if len(body) > RESULT_CAP:\n                    body = body[:RESULT_CAP] + f\"\\n... ({len(body) - RESULT_CAP} more characters in the raw transcript)\"\n                out.append(f\"**Tool result**\\n\\n```\\n{body}\\n```\\n\")\n    return \"\\n\".join(out)\n\n\ndef main():\n    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()\n    ap.add_argument(\"session_id\")\n    ap.add_argument(\"--name\", default=None)\n    args = ap.parse_args()\n\n    jsonl = find_transcript(args.session_id)\n    name = args.name or args.session_id\n    OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n    md = OUT / f\"{name}.md\"\n    md.write_text(render(jsonl))\n\n    zpath = OUT / f\"{name}.zip\"\n    with zipfile.ZipFile(zpath, \"w\", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:\n        z.write(jsonl, f\"{name}/transcript.jsonl\")\n        z.write(md, f\"{name}/transcript.md\")\n        extra = jsonl.with_suffix(\"\")\n        if extra.is_dir():\n            for f in sorted(extra.rglob(\"*\")):\n                if f.is_file():\n                    z.write(f, f\"{name}/{f.relative_to(extra)}\")\n    print(f\"{zpath} ({zpath.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB)\")\n    print(f\"{md} ({md.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB)\")\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n"
}
```

So a fold must hold whole prompts: GroupKFold on prompt_id. The\nprompt order is shuffled with a fixed seed, then prompts are dealt into\nfolds in turn, which gives 30 prompts per fold.\n\nEvery experiment reads the frozen folds.csv. Changing it needs an ADR.\n\n    python -m nthl.folds data/raw/train.csv   # rebuild folds.csv\n\"\"\"\n\nimport sys\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\n\nN_FOLDS = 5\nSEED = 42\nFOLDS_CSV = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / \"folds.csv\"\n\n\ndef build_folds(train, n_folds=N_FOLDS, seed=SEED):\n    prompts = np.array(sorted(train[\"prompt_id\"].unique()))\n    order = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(len(prompts))\n    fold_of = {prompts[j]: i % n_folds for i, j in enumerate(order)}\n    folds = train[[\"id\", \"prompt_id\"]].copy()\n    folds[\"fold\"] = folds[\"prompt_id\"].map(fold_of).astype(\"int64\")\n    return folds.sort_values(\"id\").reset_index(drop=True)\n\n\ndef load_folds():\n    return pd.read_csv(FOLDS_CSV)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    build_folds(pd.read_csv(sys.argv[1])).to_csv(FOLDS_CSV, index=False)\n    print(f\"wrote {FOLDS_CSV}\")\nEOF\ngit add src/ && git commit -q -m \"feat(cv): build the prompt-grouped folds\" -m \"Whole prompts per fold, prompt order shuffled with seed 42, dealt in turn so each fold holds 30 prompts.\n\nrefs #13\" && git log --oneline -1",

Rows sum to 1. Each experiment writes two files:\n\n    outputs/<experiment>/oof.parquet    out-of-fold, one row per train passage\n    outputs/<experiment>/test.parquet   one row per test passage\n\nso any member can be blended with any other later.\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\n\nfrom nthl.labels import LABELS\n\nCOLUMNS = [\"id\", *LABELS]\n\n\ndef check_preds(df, ids=None):\n    assert list(df.columns) == COLUMNS, \"columns must be id then the 18 labels in order\"\n    assert df[\"id\"].is_unique, \"repeated id\"\n    p = df[list(LABELS)].to_numpy(dtype=float)\n    assert np.isfinite(p).all(), \"missing or infinite probability\"\n    assert (p >= 0).all() and (p <= 1).all(), \"probability outside 0 to 1\"\n    assert np.allclose(p.sum(axis=1), 1, atol=1e-4), \"a row does not sum to 1\"\n    if ids is not None:\n        assert len(df) == len(ids) and set(df[\"id\"]) == set(ids), \"ids differ from the expected set\"\n    return df\n\n\ndef to_labels(df):\n    return np.asarray(LABELS)[df[list(LABELS)].to_numpy().argmax(axis=1)]\n\n\ndef save_preds(df, path):\n    check_preds(df)\n    path = Path(path)\n    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n    df.to_parquet(path, index=False)\n\n\ndef load_preds(path):\n    return check_preds(pd.read_parquet(path))\nEOF\n.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q 2>&1 | tail -2",

# Built-in browser

The built-in browser is a real browser pane inside the Claude desktop app, separate from the person's Chrome. Its tools are named `mcp__Claude_Browser__*` when the session itself runs inside the desktop app, and `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` when the session runs in the cloud (started from the web, a phone, or the desktop app) and is linked to the person's computer. The names after the prefix are the same either way, Claude uses whichever prefix is actually present, and this skill refers to the tools by the part after the prefix.

If the only built-in browser tool present is `enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser`, Claude calls it first: it turns the built-in browser on for this conversation, and the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` tools appear once it has run.

## What the person can see

The browser pane shares the desktop app's side panel with artifacts, documents, and file previews, and the panel shows one of them at a time. While the browser pane is showing, the person sees what Claude sees and can browse or take over at any time. While something else is open in the panel, or the panel is closed, the built-in browser keeps working but the person cannot see it.

Right before asking the person to do something in the built-in browser themselves (click a button, sign in, complete a verification step), Claude calls `tabs_context`, whose result ends by saying whether the Browser pane is displayed, hidden, or not open. If the pane is not open, Claude opens the page first and checks again. If the pane is hidden, Claude first asks the person to bring the browser back in the Claude desktop app: press Cmd+Shift+B on Mac or Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows, or close whatever else is open in the side panel and click the globe icon (the Browser button). Claude then says what to do in the browser. Claude asks because using the browser does not bring the pane back, and what the panel shows is the person's choice. Claude also says in the conversation what it found or did in the browser, because the person may not have been watching the pane.

## Sign-ins persist, and they are the person's

The built-in browser keeps its own persistent profile, shared across the desktop app's sessions. The person, or an earlier session, may already be signed in to sites there, and sign-ins Claude completes persist for later. Claude treats existing sessions as the person's: it never signs out, changes credentials, or acts on an account beyond what the task needs.

## Tabs

The built-in browser has tabs. `preview_start` with a `url` opens an additional tab at that URL in one call and returns a `tabId`, leaving existing tabs untouched, so Claude prefers it over `tabs_create` followed by `navigate` when the destination is already known. `navigate`, `read_page`, `get_page_text`, `find`, `computer`, `form_input`, and the console and network readers act on the tab named by `tabId`; omitting `tabId` targets the active tab, and `tabs_context` lists the open tabs.

## Loading via ToolSearch

Claude loads the built-in browser tools in bulk, not one-by-one: if they are in the deferred list, Claude loads them all in a single ToolSearch call whose query is their full name prefix, for example `{ query: "mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__", max_results: 64 }`.

## Reading pages

Claude prefers `get_page_text` and `read_page` over screenshots for reading, because they return the page's actual text and structure rather than pixels of the visible viewport. `computer` with action "screenshot" is for when the visual layout is the point or the person asks to see the page.

## Site approvals, blocked sites, and request_access

Depending on the person's approval settings, the person may be asked to approve a site before Claude acts on it, and some sites are blocked outright. Claude waits for a pending approval rather than working around it. If a page is refused or an approval is declined, Claude tells the person and moves on rather than retrying.

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, approvals can be answered from any of the person's devices and may take a moment to arrive, and the session may also have a `request_access` tool. If a browser tool answers that the site is not allowed yet and `request_access` is present, Claude calls it with that site's URL and scope "once" (or "site" when the task will keep using that site), waits for the person's answer, and then retries the original tool. Without `request_access`, a refused site is handled as above: Claude tells the person and moves on.

## What the built-in browser cannot open

The built-in browser cannot open `file://` URLs or `localhost` servers that Claude starts itself, because those run where Claude's shell runs, which is not where the browser pane runs. To show the person HTML that Claude generated, Claude uses an artifact instead.

## When the built-in browser cannot be reached

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, the pane runs in the Claude desktop app on the person's computer while Claude runs elsewhere, so it is reachable only while that app is open and online. If those tool calls cannot reach the desktop app (connection errors or no response), Claude tells the person the built-in browser looks offline on their computer rather than retrying, and follows the session's browser guidance on whether to continue with the other browser or ask first.

Types of Notebooks

There are multiple different types of Notebooks on Kaggle.

Notebooks

The most common type is Jupyter notebooks (usually just “notebooks”). Jupyter notebooks consist of a sequence of cells, where each cell is formatted in either Markdown (for writing text) or in a programming language of your choice (for writing code). To start a notebook, click on Create > New Notebook. This will open the Notebooks editing interface.

Notebooks may be written in either R or Python. The language can be changed under the File > Language menu.

Scripts

It's also possible to create a script. Scripts are files that execute everything as code sequentially. To start a script, create a new notebook, and then change the type to Script under File > Editor Type.

Also under the File menu, you can select what type of script you would like to execute. You may write scripts in R or in Python.

You can also execute selected lines of code by highlighting the code in the editor interface and clicking the “Run” button or hitting shift-enter. Any results will be printed to the console.

RMarkdown Scripts

RMarkdown scripts are a special type of script that executes not just R code, but RMarkdown code. This is a combination of R code and Markdown editing syntax that is prefered by many R authors in our community.
